fields.Boundary: Ratio is an operating choice. It does not create more work than the input supplies.

fields.Donor and source: Trackrunner tiger beetle; hardpan between sleepers and sunlit slab edges. This donor and assembly are retained from the earlier compendium, beyond the limited playable source roster.
fields.Prepared anatomy: Long, light hip-and-limb lever structures with separately identified distal contact tips.
fields.Selection and breeding: Select reach without unnecessary moving mass, and working articulation that preserves the intended stroke. Very long but heavy extremities can be a poor high-cadence combination.
fields.Builder contribution: Match drive force, stroke travel and stance. A complete limb assembly includes its geometry; adding a separate limb-reach term must not count that length twice.
fields.Visible racing consequence: Greater travel per useful stroke on suitable ground, with different launch and load behavior from Lowstep.
fields.Hobby and trade: Sprint builders and replacement-limb makers seek selected reach bands. Non-premium individuals can still provide useful tips or another size of assembly.
fields.Boundary: This is not a promise that long legs always win or that a juvenile automatically grows into a higher product tier.

fields.Donor and source: Clockleaf planthopper; protected seepage reeds. Late juveniles are the working source in this fictional profile; adult founders provide the next cohorts. Retained earlier compendium concept.
fields.Prepared anatomy: A paired coordinating structure that constrains the relative timing of linked hind actions. It is prepared with an intact coupling interface, not merely two decorative teeth.
fields.Selection and breeding: Select consistent phase alignment, retention of that alignment through use, and a manageable useful-stage window. Adult body size is not evidence that the juvenile coupling will be best.
fields.Builder contribution: Align the paired output with the actual launch assembly. Keep leverage selection separate. Avoid overconstraining a gait that needs independently placed feet.
fields.Visible racing consequence: More closely coordinated release can reduce unwanted rotation during an intended paired launch.
fields.Hobby and trade: Synchronizer specialists can sell stage-matched components and separately retain adult founders. Scheduling and dependable preparation are valuable even without extreme peak output.
fields.Boundary: Timing precision is not a second motor, a variable-ratio gearbox or a free increase to all running cadence.

fields.Donor and source: Glassfoot stick insect; Dewglass wall and Glazed Overgrowth. Preserve clean, intact contact tissue and enough suitable adults to continue the line.
fields.Prepared anatomy: Flexible foot-contact pads prepared in identified pairs. The contact material and its orientation are separate from the leg that carries it.
fields.Selection and breeding: Select purchase under load, release time and retention of useful contact after fouling. A fast-release ordinary-grip animal may be the missing founder for a highly adhesive line.
fields.Builder contribution: Choose front, middle and rear allocations, contact area and orientation. Different pair preparations can serve one racer; matching colors are not required for mechanical compatibility.
fields.Visible racing consequence: A planted foot holds; the unloaded foot peels away and cycles. Slow release visibly interrupts a fast gait even when static grip looks impressive.
fields.Hobby and trade: Technical and fast-contact kits; replacement pairs; alternatively prepared Gripstrips. A whole brood can serve different contact-area and performance specifications.
fields.Boundary: Running pads and Gripstrips cannot both consume the same pad source. Better grip and faster release can coexist as a genuine improvement.

fields.Donor and source: Ballast mole cricket; loose ballast and root-bank habitat. Toe damage matters to immediate use without rewriting hereditary potential.
fields.Prepared anatomy: Toothed contact ends that obtain purchase through the surface rather than relying only on smooth adhesive contact.
fields.Selection and breeding: Select useful tooth geometry, release and resistance to clogging on the declared substrate. Different particle sizes can favor different preparations.
fields.Builder contribution: Choose toe exposure and pair placement. Keep hip leverage independent when the donor’s other regions supply a Lowstep assembly.
fields.Visible racing consequence: Less slip on suitable loose material; a different contact and release pattern on smooth metal.
fields.Hobby and trade: Rubble-run kits, local ash-course stock and field-supply orders. Different toes and hip structures can become disjoint products from one appropriately preserved donor.
fields.Boundary: Loose-ground performance is a surface relationship, not a permanent all-surface traction bonus.

fields.Donor and source: Kilnback scarab; Cooling compost and furnace beds. The source is internal support anatomy, not every visible outer plate.
fields.Prepared anatomy: Interlocking ribs arranged between the working roots they must support. Open spaces accommodate living tissue and articulated joints.
fields.Selection and breeding: Select load support per mass, useful deformation and dimensional consistency. A light strong brace can be a real improvement, not a compulsory trade for some unrelated weakness.
fields.Builder contribution: Orient the ribs along the intended load path. Protect articulation instead of binding every joint rigidly. A horn support and a wing-root support need not be the same pattern.
fields.Visible racing consequence: The working root moves against support rather than collapsing its surrounding body. Its benefit depends on where force is actually applied.
fields.Hobby and trade: Structural kits and custom reinforcement work. Breeders supply plates; skilled fitters arrange them for particular hosts and working organs.
fields.Boundary: It is not general armor. A rigid shell can transmit a harsh landing; suspension still has its own job.

fields.Donor and source: Rad-roach supporting plates from separately identified donor or retained native material. A starter host’s own structure is not a free duplicate product.
fields.Prepared anatomy: Overlapping small ribs linked by flexible seams, preserving motion while providing an organized supporting path.
fields.Selection and breeding: Select repeatable flex and adequate support for the intended working load. Uncontrolled softness and helpful compliance are different properties.
fields.Builder contribution: Set overlap and the joints allowed to flex. A broad soft cradle can be unsuitable for a concentrated horn-root load without additional local support.
fields.Visible racing consequence: Controlled body compliance across uneven sections, without demanding that every impact be absorbed in the legs alone.
fields.Hobby and trade: General club preparations, restorations and light custom projects. A native foundation may already provide enough support and require no replacement.
fields.Boundary: This recovered reference design is not an extra global mandatory frame swap or a claim that a living host can donate its own essential structure twice.

fields.Donor and source: Sumpfly; damp service voids, Seep ledges and the Rooted signal pole. Protect both sensing stalks.
fields.Prepared anatomy: Paired moving sensory stalks and a prepared signal junction. The anatomy remains distinct from the feet or braces that execute a correction.
fields.Selection and breeding: Select useful rotational sensitivity, signal delay and pair calibration. Useful information under motion matters more than stalk size.
fields.Builder contribution: Preserve exposure, paired orientation and connection to an available response. Fitting under an obstructive shell can defeat the selected sensitivity.
fields.Visible racing consequence: An earlier or less biased correction can begin through the host’s existing anatomy. The correction itself still needs ground contact or an appropriate airborne actuator.
fields.Hobby and trade: Fast-contact kits, Hopper builders and Flyer instrumentation. Prepared matched pairs are a useful product; unmatched single fragments are not automatically equivalent.
fields.Boundary: No passive armor, extra traction force or supernatural awareness of hidden rivals. The real reference describes halteres as rotation sensors, not stabilizing ballast.

fields.Donor and source: Saltglass mantis; Hanging frames and prey-facing Saltglass perches. The same forelimb source can instead be prepared as Catchclaws.
fields.Prepared anatomy: Articulated forelimbs configured to open into a support position; the support-only preparation has no operative grasping attack.
fields.Selection and breeding: Select useful extension, firm support and responsive folding. Giant span is not the sole goal: the brace must reach a surface in the intended posture.
fields.Builder contribution: Set its working support position and folded clearance. Distinguish a brace that is genuinely converted from a weapon merely renamed on a label.
fields.Visible racing consequence: Adds a real supporting contact when deployed. It may broaden the racer’s passing envelope during use.
fields.Hobby and trade: Speedsters-compatible support conversions where their actual capability qualifies, as well as Open stability sets and fitting commissions.
fields.Boundary: The brace does nothing to support the animal if it cannot reach a suitable surface. The donor cannot supply a second untouched forelimb pair.

fields.Donor and source: Gutterback darkling side-shell stock, allocated instead of complete Railshoes where regions overlap. This elaborates an earlier reference concept.
fields.Prepared anatomy: Rounded high contact stops on short supported mounts. Their height is selected to catch developing lean against a guide wall.
fields.Selection and breeding: Select shell integrity and support at the needed geometry. Surface smoothness is relevant to sliding but not the complete anti-lean purpose.
fields.Builder contribution: Position relative to normal body posture and wall height. Keep them clear during ordinary running if their job is only to catch a lean.
fields.Visible racing consequence: A visible contact limits further tipping when the appropriate wall exists.
fields.Hobby and trade: Narrow-channel racing, beginner handling packs and replacement stops. The same stock family can serve anti-lean products or sliding-guide products.
fields.Boundary: This is the direct contact-style stabilizer analogue. It is neither a sensory organ nor a powered corrective limb.

fields.Donor and source: Switchyard hopper hind joints; the historic product name is a workshop pattern, not a demand that a different donor be invented.
fields.Prepared anatomy: Compliant joint structures prepared for landing on retained running limbs. They do not include every structure needed for an active launch.
fields.Selection and breeding: Select useful compression travel and controlled return at the expected load. Return timing and damping are evaluated separately from maximal spring force.
fields.Builder contribution: Fit joint travel, neutral posture and available leg clearance. Too little travel reaches a hard stop; poorly controlled return can lift the animal again.
fields.Visible racing consequence: The landing compresses, the body decelerates and the limb returns to useful running geometry.
fields.Hobby and trade: Jump-course and uneven-floor kits, service replacements, or a product outlet for donors unsuitable as premium complete Hoppers.
fields.Boundary: A complete Hopper assembly already contains corresponding joint anatomy. Complete Hoppers and these joints are alternate allocations unless the construction explicitly uses different sources.

fields.Donor and source: Reservoir waxmoth larval material; Insulation larder and suitable feed cavities. A separate donor is needed when a full reservoir uses the same fatbody.
fields.Prepared anatomy: A confined moving tissue mass in a supported damping sleeve, arranged so relative motion dissipates rebound instead of freely striking the host.
fields.Selection and breeding: Select useful dissipative material and a controllable moving mass. A large recently fed larva is not automatically a well-made damper.
fields.Builder contribution: Choose mass, permitted travel, orientation and placement. The surrounding support and sleeve are part of the preparation; loose ballast is not equivalent.
fields.Visible racing consequence: Following an impact, the internal mass moves relative to the body and helps reduce continuing oscillation.
fields.Hobby and trade: Hopper sets, rough-course refinements and preparation labor. A breeder focused on damping can be distinct from a breeder focused on energy storage.
fields.Boundary: The same mass cannot simultaneously be counted as a full usable fuel store. It does not soften the incoming impact by magic before it moves.

fields.Donor and source: Reservoir waxmoth; feeding larvae in Insulation larder and related cavities. Retained adults sustain the line; the useful tissue stage is not the reproductive stage.
fields.Prepared anatomy: A prepared energy-storage organ with its own delivery interface and supported placement.
fields.Selection and breeding: Select usable storage per mass and adequate release conductance. Record fill separately. Complement a dense but restrictive line with useful delivery, not merely another heavier larva.
fields.Builder contribution: Choose position and race-start fill; match the outlet to the combined working demand. Keep posture and belly clearance in view.
fields.Visible racing consequence: Sustains work until reserve or output becomes limiting. Carrying more stored energy changes distribution and mass.
fields.Hobby and trade: Endurance kits, repeated-action builds and recurring ordinary supply. Adult breeders and harvest-stage larvae have different customers.
fields.Boundary: This is an energy source, not a new organ that independently supplies unlimited instantaneous power. Preparation is an alternative to spending the same tissue in a Keel.

fields.Donor and source: Orchard honeybee stock from protected flowering plots and managed colonies. Retained from the early compendium; it is not restricted to the limited prototype donor roster.
fields.Prepared anatomy: A fluid reserve and high-delivery outlet, prepared as one supplied component rather than an empty sac credited with unlimited energy.
fields.Selection and breeding: Select useful delivery and capacity at the intended burden. Production selection considers the actual colony’s reproductive structure; a captured pair of workers is not assumed to found it.
fields.Builder contribution: Place and support the filled crop; match demand and filling to the race. The outlet, contents and shell mass remain distinct.
fields.Visible racing consequence: Provides rapid supply for demanding starts or repeated active work while sufficient contents remain.
fields.Hobby and trade: Sprint and offensive-kit suppliers, colony specialists and breeders selling productive reproductive units.
fields.Boundary: Colony genetics and foundation details need their own donor monograph. The compendium recognizes the source without copying a pair-bred Hopper algorithm onto it.

fields.Donor and source: Ashveil moth; Felt loft and Textile Ruins. Preserve intact margins and the supporting veins.
fields.Prepared anatomy: Paired shaped wing-derived surfaces mounted as passive vanes, with declared orientation and a supported root.
fields.Selection and breeding: Select useful stiffness, surface form, mass and resistance for the intended speed range. Color pattern can be desirable independently.
fields.Builder contribution: Set angle and exposure without blocking the head or surrounding grafts. The useful loaded shape matters more than its unloaded outline alone.
fields.Visible racing consequence: Changes aerodynamic load and pitch tendency while moving. Its resistance is a real interaction, not an unrelated penalty.
fields.Hobby and trade: Ground speed kits, custom silhouettes and material selections. Particular markings can motivate collector editions without extra race power.
fields.Boundary: A passive vane does not grant sustained flight; useful effects at RRR’s eventual physical scale require deliberate authored calibration.

fields.Donor and source: Separate head-shell plates from Bullhorn stock, where the harvest preserves those plates independently of the ram.
fields.Prepared anatomy: A shaped shell surface spanning or splitting around the brow. Its root transfers air load into supporting anatomy.
fields.Selection and breeding: Select plate shape, stiffness and mass for a preparation. The donor’s horn length does not determine foil quality.
fields.Builder contribution: Choose a central or divided configuration around other grafts. A horn and a split foil can coexist when their roots and operating clearances actually fit.
fields.Visible racing consequence: Motion produces a visible attitude/load effect; it does not hold the nose down while stationary through an invisible aura.
fields.Hobby and trade: Ground aero sets and custom horn-bearing builds. Disjoint head plates provide a different product from the same adequately preserved source animal.
fields.Boundary: The source family is front aero, not head armor by default. Any real protective coverage is evaluated separately.

fields.Donor and source: Sandfelt moth; Dry Feltworks and Felt loft. Preserve the resilient ventral material rather than judging the animal only by wing appearance.
fields.Prepared anatomy: A contact pad with compliant support and an adjustable mounting stalk. Material and clearance are different parts of the construction.
fields.Selection and breeding: Select appropriate friction, behavior after fouling and compression travel. The highest friction is not automatically the fastest complete setup.
fields.Builder contribution: Set whether and where the pad engages a raised approach. Keep ordinary running clearance and passive-launch geometry distinct from the material’s own properties.
fields.Visible racing consequence: Contact removes motion; the pad compresses within its working travel. Out of contact it produces no braking force.
fields.Hobby and trade: Approach kits, pad replacement stock and custom fitting. A dependable mid-range material can be commercially valuable across many ordinary setups.
fields.Boundary: Braking does not refill a reservoir or improve genes. A missed approach can come from fitting even with excellent material.

fields.Donor and source: Glassfoot contact pads allocated to braking rather than an additional running contact set.
fields.Prepared anatomy: A supported strip of gripping material arranged under the racer with a known contact direction and clearance.
fields.Selection and breeding: Select the material behavior appropriate to the approach surface. Running-foot release remains a useful clue but is not automatically a separate braking-stat bonus.
fields.Builder contribution: Choose strip area, support and engagement. The preparation changes how existing anatomy is used, not its hereditary identity.
fields.Visible racing consequence: Deceleration begins when the strip touches the intended surface. Too much engagement can remove more pace than intended.
fields.Hobby and trade: Alternative output from a contact-breeding line, inexpensive approach experiments and ordinary braking orders.
fields.Boundary: One pad source has one current use. Keeping the source animal for breeding remains a distinct choice.

fields.Donor and source: Gutterback darkling; Underpipe Aprons and Ballast trench. Observe controlled glancing contact rather than assuming a shiny shell is low-loss.
fields.Prepared anatomy: Paired sliding side-shell surfaces with mounts that carry a stated range of contact load.
fields.Selection and breeding: Select low sliding loss together with adequate support and useful mass. A smooth but unsupported shell may complement a strong rough line as breeding stock.
fields.Builder contribution: Set working width, height and exposure. Consider passing space and the likely rail contact on the intended course.
fields.Visible racing consequence: The guide, rather than an unsuitable exposed surface, meets the wall. Reduced sliding loss matters only during that contact.
fields.Hobby and trade: Guided-track kits, club service parts and carefully measured rail-material lines. Ordinary stock can serve beginner guides or alternate Guardknuckle patterns.
fields.Boundary: Native shell contact still exists. Guides are not a permission to enter the track and do not award free speed away from its wall.

fields.Donor and source: Ballast mole-cricket joint-lining regions allocated without counting tissue already included in a complete hip assembly. New detailed preparation of a previously named joint-support function.
fields.Prepared anatomy: Flexible bearing surfaces and protective sleeve tissue around an articulating connection; a sleeve must support motion rather than bind it.
fields.Selection and breeding: Select low working resistance, useful travel and protection from grit. A tight seal that arrests the joint is not a superior product.
fields.Builder contribution: Fit the actual joint and expected motion range. Declare whether a complete Lowstep already includes the necessary lining before adding another preparation.
fields.Visible racing consequence: Less avoidable loss and contamination at that specific joint. It does not increase output at every unrelated organ.
fields.Hobby and trade: Maintenance supplies, precision fitting and dirty-course kits. Replacing a worn interface can restore performance without altering any genome.
fields.Boundary: This completes the bearing-like function in the compendium; it is not a claim that another runtime item was added this wave.

fields.Donor and source: Switchyard hopper; Split-sleeper bank and related grass margins. Keep both sides of the intended pair intact.
fields.Prepared anatomy: A complete hind-limb system: running geometry, loadable elastic elements, release coordination and landing joints. Its load path remains connected to the host.
fields.Selection and breeding: Select return, synchronization and controlled settling as distinct contributions. An ordinary jumper with an exceptional missing contribution can be a valuable founder.
fields.Builder contribution: Set preload, launch geometry, pair alignment and the intended circumstances for commitment. Stored work must be available; excessive launch is not automatically desirable.
fields.Visible racing consequence: The hind limbs load, release, clear an actual obstacle or rival, recontact a real surface and recover running. Each phase visibly uses the fitted anatomy.
fields.Hobby and trade: Signature racing tins, intermediate kit stock, selected breeders and joint-only alternative preparations. The founding style remains relevant at both local and elite levels.
fields.Boundary: No automatic passing, remote obstacle erasure or guaranteed jump-win. The action entry below defines what the actual anatomy must achieve.

fields.Donor and source: Bullhorn beetle; Compost undercrofts and Cooling compost. Protect the supported root as carefully as the striking tip.
fields.Prepared anatomy: A curved contact horn with root reinforcement; different shapes push, lift or glance in different ways.
fields.Selection and breeding: Select a useful contact shape, root integrity and retained function after impacts. Maximum length is not a universal target.
fields.Builder contribution: Align the ram with its supported force path and intended approach. Provide clearances for nearby vanes and head movement.
fields.Visible racing consequence: The racer gains position through an actual aligned encounter. Contact changes both bodies; recovery follows the force transmitted.
fields.Hobby and trade: Open and Fireworks builds, founder-style collections and custom horn shaping. Ordinary horns can be ideal for smaller bodies.
fields.Boundary: A horn does not provide motor output or a homing attack. It must reach the opponent.

fields.Donor and source: Saltglass mantis; Hanging frames and Saltglass perches. Preserve the opposing working surfaces and the closing joints.
fields.Prepared anatomy: Articulated grasping arms with a close, hold and release range. They are not permanently extended decorative blades.
fields.Selection and breeding: Select closure at the intended reach, useful hold and reliable release. Long arms with late closure can miss the intended interception.
fields.Builder contribution: Arrange reach, supported load and clearance from running limbs. A grip that traps the attacker in traffic may be a poor racing choice.
fields.Visible racing consequence: An actual arm closes on reachable anatomy, holds or disrupts it, then releases and returns. Contact may damage exposed structures in the eventual chosen damage model.
fields.Hobby and trade: Offensive kits, reactive builds and selected-arm lines. Counterbrace preparation is an alternative use, not a second untouched pair.
fields.Boundary: It is not a universal counter to every horn or a ranged stun. Closing before contact and closing after the target passes have different outcomes.

fields.Donor and source: Kilnback outer protective plates, distinguished from its internal Boxbrace source. Allocation must preserve actual nonoverlapping material.
fields.Prepared anatomy: Overlapping shell plates around specified body regions with flexible breaks at working joints.
fields.Selection and breeding: Select resistance to the intended contact, useful coverage and articulation at a suitable mass. Protecting a region and bracing a root are different objectives.
fields.Builder contribution: Choose exposed regions to cover; preserve vents, sensing and limb travel. A fitted shell map records which regions remain vulnerable.
fields.Visible racing consequence: A strike meets a particular plate or an uncovered joint. Protection alters the contact locally rather than absorbing all damage into a universal shield.
fields.Hobby and trade: Open protection kits, replacement plates, custom armor fitting and show finishes. Fireworks permits only its declared light-protection class.
fields.Boundary: Armor is an RRR-native extension of shell construction. Its detailed damage coefficients and broad death policy are not settled by this reference.

fields.Donor and source: Caustic bombardier; earlier compendium drain-edge and damp-stone habitat. This is a fictional racing form, not a chemical-handling guide.
fields.Prepared anatomy: A gland, valves and directional outlets prepared as a self-contained spray assembly, with finite contents and a defined recharge requirement.
fields.Selection and breeding: Select repeatable pulses, sound valves and useful outlet geometry. A large sac does not prove dependable delivery.
fields.Builder contribution: Orient the outlet for the intended encounter and separate its contents from the drive’s metabolic budget. Mounting must protect the racer from its own discharge.
fields.Visible racing consequence: A visible, reachable target intersects an actual pulse. Contents deplete and the assembly recovers according to its preparation.
fields.Hobby and trade: Fireworks specialists, rear-defense constructions and limited-output breeder lines. Ordinary dependable glands can be preferable to erratic large ones.
fields.Boundary: No real reagent recipe, invisible unlimited ammunition, remote damage roll or automatic reclassification as a motor.

fields.Donor and source: Glasswing dragonfly; cooling ponds with clear emergence edges. Juvenile aquatic rearing, intact emergence and adult reproductive stock have distinct needs.
fields.Prepared anatomy: Four wing surfaces and their working roots. A complete Flyer also needs driving muscles, coordinated leverage, supply and sensory control.
fields.Selection and breeding: Select useful wing work, torsional response and root endurance. Decorative brilliance is not a flight-efficiency assay.
fields.Builder contribution: Provide working sweep, supported hinges and adequate supply. Dorsal armor can be shaped around flight roots rather than prohibited solely by its name.
fields.Visible racing consequence: Produces sustained powered movement through air when the complete system can support it; it does not merely make a ground hop last longer.
fields.Hobby and trade: Flyer kits, wing-pair specialists, emergence services and stage-sensitive transport. The entire hobby supply chain is relevant even before a flight engine is built.
fields.Boundary: No direct PCR wing-slot equivalence: passive front aero and powered flight remain different systems. Full aerial dynamics are downstream implementation work.

fields.Donor and source: Longwing locust stock in exposed grass and reed margins; retained earlier compendium concept. Exact world placement and full donor monograph remain to be authored.
fields.Prepared anatomy: Long paired flight surfaces with folding and root articulation suited to forward travel. A complete package identifies its driving and sensory requirements.
fields.Selection and breeding: Select sustained useful wing work, reliable folding and root geometry. Maximum span alone does not establish a good gate racer.
fields.Builder contribution: Arrange folded carrying width, working sweep and a drive linkage matched to the surfaces. Keep pitch control and powered lift separately understandable.
fields.Visible racing consequence: Longer forward flight strokes and different gate-approach behavior from the maneuver-oriented Quadwing construction.
fields.Hobby and trade: Forward-flight specialists, compact transport preparations and alternative Flyer kits. The design gives a different reason to breed flight stock rather than a higher numbered dragonfly.
fields.Boundary: This is a current reference design, not a newly populated Wildlands species or implemented aerial event.

fields.Donor and source: Click-beetle stock from the earlier recovery concept; exact named population remains a donor-monograph task.
fields.Prepared anatomy: A loaded hinge and release arrangement that can change a toppled host’s posture when it has suitable support and clearance.
fields.Selection and breeding: Select usable recovery work and reliable latch release at the intended body load. A stronger snap is not automatically a controlled recovery.
fields.Builder contribution: Place the hinge so its action can right the particular host; avoid inventing support beneath an animal suspended in the air.
fields.Visible racing consequence: An interrupted racer performs a distinct self-righting action and pays its real lost time and resource use.
fields.Hobby and trade: Recovery specialists, exhibition builds and Open insurance against a particular class of disruption.
fields.Boundary: It is neither a universal resurrection organ nor a steerable long-range Hopper. Injury and permanent-loss policy remain separate.

sections.title: 5. Race action lexicon: what anatomy visibly does
sections.intro: These entries specify causes, commitments, interactions and readable outcomes. They do not prescribe a solver, animation frame count or numerical success roll. A real-time implementation, an abstract simulation and an illustrated handbook must describe the same action.

fields.Required anatomy and situation: Useful feet, working limbs, drive, coordination and supply; native anatomy already provides a complete running system.
fields.Causal sequence: A contact plants, available work loads it, the body advances, that contact unloads and releases, and another useful support continues the gait. Maintaining pace is repeated successful delivery, not repeated purchase of a speed bonus.
fields.Builder or breeder influence: Drive cadence and force, foot release, stride geometry, moving mass and supply create different improvement opportunities. An efficient new drive can sustain the same output longer; a quicker foot can remove a gait bottleneck.
fields.Interference and unsuccessful outcomes: Loose footing, obstructed travel, limited supply or a heavily loaded body can limit useful output. The result must not imply the animal lacks a motor when its feet are actually stuck.
fields.Recognition: Step frequency, stroke reach, slipping and recovery belong to the visible construction. A fast racer should visibly travel fast; the presentation must not diminish speed or winning into a lesson about diagnostics.

fields.Required anatomy and situation: Contact and articulated anatomy capable of redirecting the body within the available racing space.
fields.Causal sequence: The animal changes its support and working strokes, redirects momentum and continues into the next part of the course. Wall contact may assist, obstruct or dissipate motion according to the actual geometry.
fields.Builder or breeder influence: Stance, body proportions, contact material, native articulation and supported correction matter. A high-cadence motor does not alone specify a turning radius.
fields.Interference and unsuccessful outcomes: Traffic can occupy a desired line; an exposed graft can clip a wall; inadequate contact can cause outward loss. A fixed penalty applied at every bend cannot stand in for all these distinct meanings.
fields.Recognition: The body and feet orient into the turn. A held wide brace or guide remains in the actual width of the racer rather than vanishing to permit a pass.

entries.title: Detect and correct a developing lean

fields.Required anatomy and situation: An available cue, an appropriate controller or reflex, and an actual corrective contact or actuator. A passive stop instead acts through contact without an active sensing requirement.
fields.Causal sequence: Disturbance occurs; sensing or mechanical contact registers it; available anatomy responds; the body returns toward useful support or continues into failure.
fields.Builder or breeder influence: Sensor delay changes when correction can begin. Brace range changes what surface can be reached. Body and root support determine whether the response can carry the load.
fields.Interference and unsuccessful outcomes: A sensor cannot correct while its only response limb is committed to gripping an opponent. A brace cannot push against empty air. These outcomes follow the construction, not a universal immunity state.
fields.Recognition: Distinguish a small anticipatory foot correction, an extended support, and a hard Guardknuckle touching a wall. They should not all play the same generic balance sparkle.

fields.Required anatomy and situation: A prepared contact surface, adequate support and a matching surface within reach. Native limb deceleration is a different available action.
fields.Causal sequence: The pad reaches the approach, compresses within its travel, dissipates motion while contact persists, then disengages or continues to drag if set too low.
fields.Builder or breeder influence: Material and support are donor/preparation properties; height, area and approach setup are builder choices. Both determine the working contact.
fields.Interference and unsuccessful outcomes: A raised pad misses the surface. A worn or fouled pad behaves differently. Excess contact can lose unnecessary pace. None of these directly mutates the donor line.
fields.Recognition: The visible pad touches before slowing is credited. A passively airborne racer is not secretly braking against the ground below it.

fields.Required anatomy and situation: An aligned reachable rival, useful closing motion, supported horn root and adequate contact to deliver the approach.
fields.Causal sequence: Align; brace the working structure; approach; horn or opponent makes contact; load transfers into both constructions; separate or remain engaged; recover useful running.
fields.Builder or breeder influence: Horn geometry determines contact opportunities. Drive and traction supply the approach. Root and frame support determine how much of it becomes a useful interaction.
fields.Interference and unsuccessful outcomes: A rival can move out of reach, brace, intercept, jump or absorb the contact locally. A long horn can miss useful purchase. No specific module grants universal victory over every other.
fields.Recognition: Contact is visible at an actual point and the attacker also responds. A missed charge does not damage a remote rival because the animation finished.

fields.Required anatomy and situation: Available grasping arms, a reachable object, enough closing time and a support path for the resulting load.
fields.Causal sequence: Present the grasp envelope; close around actual anatomy; hold or redirect within available leverage; release; recover the folded or running arrangement.
fields.Builder or breeder influence: Closure speed, reach, gripping shape and release control define the opportunity. Extra dedicated arms need not remove the native forefeet; replacing forelegs may do so. The exact build decides the locomotion cost.
fields.Interference and unsuccessful outcomes: An early close catches nothing; a late close misses; holding can slow both racers. An opponent can break alignment or force a poor load path. A rendered grip is not automatic immobilization.
fields.Recognition: The arms occupy space throughout opening, contact and return. A folded arm, a prepared brace and an open trap have distinct silhouettes.

entries.title: Load and execute an active hop

fields.Required anatomy and situation: A complete launch-capable assembly, a support surface, available work, useful clearance, and a planned recontact opportunity. The roach does not need a rival to use it.
fields.Causal sequence: Adopt a loading posture; store work; retain or relax the preload; release through synchronized hind action; leave the support; follow the resulting trajectory; prepare the landing; recover running.
fields.Builder or breeder influence: Return determines usable stored energy; synchronization affects unwanted rotation; fitting determines launch orientation; settling affects recovery. Lower preload can be useful for a nearby clearance even with an exceptional high-capacity assembly.
fields.Interference and unsuccessful outcomes: A target may move before release; a ceiling may block the trajectory; a landing may become crowded. The animal can abandon a commitment before release under its behavioral policy, with elapsed work and time retained. After takeoff, control depends on actual available anatomy.
fields.Recognition: Loaded joints shorten or bow before release. Airborne legs reposition for landing. A high-quality motion interpretation shows commitment and outcome without requiring gigantic jumps every time.

entries.title: Leave a ramp without active jumping

fields.Required anatomy and situation: Ground speed and a course shape that redirects or removes support. A native roach can become airborne without a Hopper module.
fields.Causal sequence: The body approaches; course contact changes velocity and support; the animal leaves the lip; it travels through air and seeks valid recontact.
fields.Builder or breeder influence: Approach speed, brake contact, posture, body mass distribution and passive aero can influence the trajectory. Active jumping is only additional work if the build actually performs it.
fields.Interference and unsuccessful outcomes: Loss of useful route, excessive landing demand or a collision can prevent valid completion. A specific prototype retiring every airborne bend is not the world definition of all airborne movement.
fields.Recognition: The launch originates at the course. No unexplained hind-spring loading or second energy pulse should be shown when it did not occur.

fields.Required anatomy and situation: A reachable surface, a usable body attitude, actual receiving contacts and support for the load.
fields.Causal sequence: Place receiving limbs; contact; compress available travel; dissipate or redirect energy; return toward useful stance; resume the next work cycle.
fields.Builder or breeder influence: Landing joints manage travel and load; a Keel reduces continuing oscillation; feet establish purchase. Better sensing can prepare contact earlier but does not replace these structures.
fields.Interference and unsuccessful outcomes: A spring can rebound; a hard stop can transmit a harsh impulse; feet can skid; a poor attitude can contact the shell instead of the intended legs. The eventual injury model determines damage, not an assumed universal health tax.
fields.Recognition: Compression precedes recovery. Rapid settling is a shorter visible interruption, not an instantaneous teleport back to full running.

fields.Required anatomy and situation: A wall within reach of a supported guide or native shell and a direction of motion along that wall.
fields.Causal sequence: Contact loads the exposed surface; motion slides along it; friction and support determine the loss; separation ends that interaction.
fields.Builder or breeder influence: Guide material changes sliding loss. Working width and height determine when it meets the wall. Available support determines how much contact the guide can manage.
fields.Interference and unsuccessful outcomes: A soft unsupported root can let the shell take the remaining load. A guide cannot improve a noncontact section merely because it remains equipped.
fields.Recognition: The rail-side surface is actually present at the contact. Guiding is not indistinguishable from an invisible magnet pulling the racer through bends.

fields.Required anatomy and situation: An integrated flight system: working wings, drive, wing-root leverage, support, supply and control. Passive vanes and an active hop are insufficient by themselves.
fields.Causal sequence: Generate working wing motion; produce the needed aerodynamic force; adjust it through root and surface control; traverse the aerial course; transition to supported landing or continued flight.
fields.Builder or breeder influence: Wing work, root response, drive efficiency, supply and body distribution determine capabilities. Ground-running contact becomes important again at launch or landing, not as a free airborne traction stat.
fields.Interference and unsuccessful outcomes: Surfaces can strike gates, lose useful orientation or exceed available output. Disturbance is addressed through actual control authority. Flight competitors obey aerial route completion, not direct travel to the finish.
fields.Recognition: Wing roots and the body’s attitude express the maneuver. A hovering gate approach and sustained forward travel need different motion, not a ground sprite raised a few pixels.

fields.Required anatomy and situation: Usable native legs or a fitted recovery assembly with the necessary support, room and stored or supplied work.
fields.Causal sequence: Find support; load the available recovery mechanism; alter body attitude; re-establish feet; resume the race only after a valid recovery.
fields.Builder or breeder influence: Body shape, useful latch geometry, sufficient force and clearance determine whether the method can work.
fields.Interference and unsuccessful outcomes: A trapped or suspended roach cannot use a surface it does not reach. Structural damage may remove the available method. No arbitrary recovery cooldown replaces the physical sequence.
fields.Recognition: An extended leg recovery and a Kickback snap are visibly different. Neither erases distance already lost.

fields.Native competence: The host already runs, senses obstacles and responds to ordinary support changes. A beginner does not have to buy a brain module to make a complete kit move.
fields.Builder configuration: Placement, preload, stance, outlet orientation and other physical settings alter what the body can do. They are neither learned skills nor inherited genes.
fields.Handling and conditioning: Familiarity with release, noise, cases and newly fitted movement can affect preparedness. Conditioning should address a named behavior or response rather than add an invisible permanent motor tier.
fields.Race plan: A lanista can favor clean passing, selective contact, early preparation or another supported tendency. This expresses the desired use of anatomy; it cannot cause impossible knowledge or physically unavailable actions.
fields.Live intervention: Whether and how the player can issue in-race cues remains a separate interaction decision. The compendium does not require direct steering, a fixed token pool or an input on every corner.
fields.Course knowledge: A body can react only to actual cues or prior familiarization. Rules officials determine checkpoint validity; this does not mean the insect reads a hidden checkpoint list or knows an opponent’s genome.

sections.title: 6. Breeding objectives, morphological variation and productive habitats
sections.intro: A breeder pursues an outcome in offspring, not a larger generic quality score. The material, shape, development and present condition of an animal must remain distinguishable from the work performed by a fitter.

entries.title: Five causes that must not be conflated

fields.Inherited contribution: The potential for anatomy, material and other declared traits. It is the subject of selective breeding.
fields.Development: Whether an individual forms usable tissue under its actual growth conditions. A cramped emergence can damage a promising wing without changing the underlying inheritance.
fields.Present condition: Fill, fatigue, fouling, maturity and injury where those apply. They change current usefulness; a full crop does not prove higher inherited capacity.
fields.Preparation: The arrangement, preservation and shaping that turn actual source anatomy into a usable component. It can reveal, preserve or redirect value without inventing a new germline.
fields.Fitting: The host-specific assembly and settings. A carefully aligned parent does not produce offspring already aligned to a different customer’s roach.

entries.title: Different breeding projects deserve different stock

fields.Complement project: Add synchronization to a high-return Hopper line. Retain the missing contribution even in an individually modest jumper.
fields.Direct improvement project: Improve drive efficiency while retaining acceptable cadence and force. Genuine better output at the same burden remains desirable.
fields.Production project: Increase the proportion of usable standard components through dependable reproduction and development. Eggs alone are not finished products.
fields.Fit project: Produce useful anatomy within a repeated host or kit envelope. Similar adult size is insufficient if the working roots or motion differ.
fields.Collection project: Develop recognizable natural banding or form. Appearance can be the primary objective without claiming a racing advantage.
fields.Hereditary boundary: The current working branch keeps donor and host breeding distinct. Assimilating a horn does not automatically place a copy of that paid horn in every offspring, and graft compatibility does not establish reproductive compatibility.

entries.title: A habitat is a source, not a trait-granting machine

fields.Population: People can return for new cohorts, unrelated founders and a different useful stage. A population’s ecology and history can influence available variation without tailoring itself to the player’s current target.
fields.Field evidence: A track, molt, movement or contact mark is evidence under its actual conditions. Detailed observation and paid expertise can improve understanding; repeated looking does not force a favorable genetic outcome.
fields.Quick and detailed routes: A brief collection service and a personally explored patch may represent the same source or different nearby populations. The compendium requires the relationship to be named; it does not canonize the prototype’s duplicate-source separation.
fields.Desired anatomy: An acquisition method is selected for the tissue it must preserve: matched limbs, intact wing margins, contact pads, sensory stalks or whole reproductive stock.
fields.Return choice: The catch can become a racer, a breeder, a donor, a collectible, a sale or a released animal. A species discovery does not give ownership of its future bodies.

entries.title: Facilities express life history and production intent

fields.Dry-bank rearing: Provides appropriate refuge, laying places, limb-growth space and adult holding for the supported terrestrial profile. The same box does not automatically serve predators or aquatic stages.
fields.Deep-substrate rearing: Provides sufficient substrate, resources and access for burrowing juveniles, with adult holding handled according to the actual form.
fields.Root-to-adult cabinet: Connects a juvenile feeding system to emergence and adult reproduction. An adult-only cicada cage is a holding facility, not a complete productive line.
fields.Vertical molt case: Provides hanging and separation space for growing appendages or stage-specific coordinating anatomy. Quantity without working clearance can reduce intact output.
fields.Predator partitions: Separate incompatible animals and permit controlled reproductive contact. Their value is preserved stock and viable output, not a free bonus to inherited aggression.
fields.Larval/pupal drawer: Permits allocation between harvest-stage tissue and retained adults. Harvesting every useful larva removes the intended reproductive replacements.
fields.Pond/emergence system: Links aquatic growth, emergence support, wing expansion and adult holding. Intact wing yield requires more than a water tank.
fields.Colony nursery: Separates productive members, reproductive structure and provisioning. It requires a dedicated donor model rather than copying a two-worker pairing rule.
fields.Common rule: A facility changes conditions, care burden, output reliability or feasible life stages. It does not select the best allele or add inherited speed because it is expensive.

entries.title: Line identity is not a guarantee

fields.Line: An intentionally maintained ancestry and selection project. Its name can develop recognition through repeatable observed output and history.
fields.Brood: A particular reproductive cohort. Several measurements from one animal do not create several descendants; several siblings do not create several independent broods.
fields.Observed claim: State what was measured, under what conditions and among which recorded descendants. Unmeasured animals remain unknown, not automatic failures or successes.
fields.Changing objective: A new selection objective may found a branch or a revised line. A catalogued revision number is not automatically a count of generations.
fields.Ordinary use: Casual buying and ordinary surplus sales do not require research-grade pedigree paperwork. Evidence becomes valuable where a customer’s particular promise needs it.

fields.Status and source: New qualitative morphology proposal for Bullhorn stock. Inheritance and prevalence require a dedicated donor expansion; none is asserted as an implemented mutation.
fields.Physical difference: A divided working horn shape supported by one joined root.
fields.Purpose: Different simultaneous contact opportunities or a stronger purchase on a narrow appendage.
fields.Selection and construction: Select useful geometry and root support; prepare its actual contact surfaces.
fields.Non-equivalence: Two tips do not each receive the full force of two independent charges.

fields.Status and source: New qualitative morphology proposal for Glassfoot stock. Inheritance and prevalence require a dedicated donor expansion; none is asserted as an implemented mutation.
fields.Physical difference: Shallow channels dividing the active contact material.
fields.Purpose: A new contact/fouling pattern that may retain usable purchase in a particular contaminated surface state.
fields.Selection and construction: Measure purchase, release and fouling recovery together; do not infer performance from the attractive pattern.
fields.Non-equivalence: Channels do not guarantee universal self-cleaning or a fixed high-tier label.

fields.Status and source: New qualitative morphology proposal for Hopper stock. Inheritance and prevalence require a dedicated donor expansion; none is asserted as an implemented mutation.
fields.Physical difference: A joint structure with successive working deformation ranges.
fields.Purpose: Different response to small surface disturbances and larger landing loads.
fields.Selection and construction: Select and measure the useful progression; fit within its actual travel.
fields.Non-equivalence: It does not store or release the same launch energy twice, and it is not inherently better at every load.

fields.Status and source: New qualitative morphology proposal for Ashveil stock. Inheritance and prevalence require a dedicated donor expansion; none is asserted as an implemented mutation.
fields.Physical difference: A veined surface that can open along a defined split.
fields.Purpose: Passive aero and a possible separately supported deployment pattern with distinct open/closed geometry.
fields.Selection and construction: Breed the structural form; prepare and configure the actuation rather than assuming shape alone supplies it.
fields.Non-equivalence: A movable surface still needs a mechanism to open; a louver is not powered flight.

fields.Status and source: New qualitative morphology proposal for Scarab stock. Inheritance and prevalence require a dedicated donor expansion; none is asserted as an implemented mutation.
fields.Physical difference: Plate segments whose boundaries preserve useful limb or dorsal movement.
fields.Purpose: Protection can coexist with movement through a different overlap arrangement.
fields.Selection and construction: Select plate properties and usable seams; tailor the final coverage to the host.
fields.Non-equivalence: A visible seam may remain a vulnerability. Plate coverage is local, not a universal shield.

fields.Status and source: New qualitative morphology proposal for A declared donor or host line. Inheritance and prevalence require a dedicated donor expansion; none is asserted as an implemented mutation.
fields.Physical difference: A recognizable natural pattern that persists through its specified life stage.
fields.Purpose: Collection identity, breeder recognition and coordinated visual kits.
fields.Selection and construction: Select inherited pattern where the form’s model supports it; distinguish applied finish and developmental variation.
fields.Non-equivalence: Color grants no automatic speed, genetic certificate or fixed sale premium.

sections.title: 7. Grafting, swapping and the life of a component
sections.intro: Swappable living parts are central to RRR. The proposed common workshop practice below protects that identity without converting the host into an indestructible machine or imposing an unexplained injury roll on every routine rebuild. This chapter advances D03/D04 qualitatively; exact times, loss rates, regrowth and lifetime policy remain separate decisions.

entries.title: Assimilation is innate; preparation is expertise

fields.Raw grafting: The defining mutation can incorporate suitable insect anatomy without a licensed commercial kit. This preserves the founding horn-and-pincers improvisation.
fields.Prepared grafting: A fitter selects the source, exposes a useful root, supplies support and arranges a repeatable interface. The preparation improves usability and predictability; it does not confer permission to assimilate.
fields.Working readiness: Attachment, supply and useful motion may become ready at different points. A root that has seated is not proof that every high-load action is ready. The visual and care state should make the distinction legible.
fields.Accessibility: A beginner tin and a competent local Wrangloid provide a dependable route to an ordinary build. Requiring rare surgery skills for every legal kit contradicts the mass-market hobby.
fields.Freedom: Expert custom roots and improvised assemblies can exceed commercial patterns. Their difficulties come from actual support, clearance and supply, not a species rejection list.

entries.title: A maintained exchange boundary supports repeated rebuilding

fields.Common workshop profile: Prepared sects with intact exchange boundaries can be detached, supported and refitted through the declared ordinary service procedure. Rebuilding is a normal hobby activity, not inherently a gamble that destroys a prized collection.
fields.Raw constructions: A fully merged improvised structure may lack a prepared release boundary. Its removal requires an appropriate handling decision rather than the assumption that every graft detaches identically.
fields.Native material: Where native anatomy was displaced and retained, it is actual retained material. Where it was consumed, regrowth or a replacement must have its own explanation; a menu choice cannot conjure it.
fields.Condition: Damaged roots, inadequate preservation or obstructed motion can make a particular swap more demanding. Those causes are named. No universal per-swap damage tax is adopted here.
fields.Commercial effect: Prepared components support second-hand trade, borrowing, repair services and multi-build collections. A seller distinguishes the source history and present interface condition from the component’s original pedigree.

entries.title: Four material states with different meanings

fields.Working on a host: Integrated anatomy uses that host’s support and supply. Its current setup belongs to the fitted construction.
fields.Buffered living sect: Removed tissue is held in an appropriate support and maintenance environment. It is not undergoing ordinary whole-donor development as if still attached to the original animal.
fields.Prepared structural material: Shell-derived rigid or elastic material may retain physical utility under different conditions from an active organ. The living root and the structural part are not always the same material.
fields.Spent or damaged material: A part can lose a working function while retaining another use: appearance, study, restoration reference or a salvage preparation explicitly supported by the remaining anatomy.
fields.No universal shelf rule: Neither infinite shelf life nor rapid spoilage for every component is established. A preservation class names what must remain intact and how readiness is restored; exact durations belong to later material profiles.

entries.title: Donor stage and graft maintenance are separate histories

fields.Before preparation: The donor’s stage determines which anatomy exists and what future role the animal can serve. A waxmoth adult is not a larval fatbody order.
fields.After preparation: The removed component has its own condition and maintenance history. Its parent animal aging in another enclosure does not transform that detached component automatically.
fields.Integrated growth: How a host maintains or remodels a graft must be specified by the graft’s profile. Assimilation is not permission for unlimited renewal of rare material or automatic improvement with age.
fields.Juvenile preparations: A stage-specific Lockstep remains useful only if the preparation preserves the required working structure. Its availability before extraction and its viability afterward are different design questions.
fields.Supply implication: Breeders can sell target-stage stock, prepared inventory or adults for reproduction. These are not interchangeable products with the same transport requirements.

entries.title: Keep consequence without making every hobby a care chore

fields.Purposeful care: Maintains an animal, a graft, a productive brood or a valuable condition. Each care practice names its affected object.
fields.Routine support: Approved care presets, hired boarding, common feed and standard preservation let casual hobbyists own attractive racers without repeated compulsory clicks.
fields.Expert work: Specific conditioning, stage management, preparation and selection offer additional depth where they change a useful outcome.
fields.Consequence: Failing a real requirement can damage stock, interrupt production or lose a race according to the later agreed condition model. It does not automatically destroy unrelated facilities and collections.
fields.Unresolved policy: Global aging, permanent death, broad injury and regenerative limits remain explicitly open. Defining repeatable workshop swaps does not settle all of them.

sections.title: 8. Set architecture, product families and complete projects
sections.intro: A coordinated set is desirable because it solves a construction problem, gives it a recognizable identity and supplies the actual parts. The source kit/upgrade distinction supports complete host tins and conversion sets without assuming a universal set bonus. [W14.S05] [W14.S06]

fields.Declared contents: A Lowline host; native drive, linkage, reserve and joints; selected contact or guide upgrades according to the printed edition.
fields.Why the combination works: The guide teaches visible placement and a useful first change without requiring a complete organ replacement.
fields.Breeding and commercial purpose: Ordinary whole hosts and dependable stock can sustain affordable kit supply. A beginner chooses finish and name immediately.
fields.Edition rule: A named set is a family of printed specifications, not ownership of particular source insects. A complete tin includes a host; a conversion set explicitly does not. Substitutions require the intended function, measured suitability and actual fit.

fields.Declared contents: Needleback host; Cicada Redline and quick-release contact set; all omitted functions identified as native.
fields.Why the combination works: The feet must let the drive’s cadence become useful steps. Narrow body space does not shrink the prepared parts.
fields.Breeding and commercial purpose: A maker selects host geometry and supplied-foot performance; a breeder can work specifically on release or efficient drive.
fields.Edition rule: A named set is a family of printed specifications, not ownership of particular source insects. A complete tin includes a host; a conversion set explicitly does not. Substitutions require the intended function, measured suitability and actual fit.

fields.Product purpose: Responsive contact rather than maximum stickiness.
fields.Declared contents: Contact preparations plus Gyropods and a host with actual available correction anatomy.
fields.Why the combination works: Feet establish useful contact and release. Sensing helps start a correction but supplies none of its force.
fields.Breeding and commercial purpose: Contact breeders and sensor suppliers can trade through one recognizable conversion set. A higher-price sensor cannot compensate for unusable feet.
fields.Edition rule: A named set is a family of printed specifications, not ownership of particular source insects. A complete tin includes a host; a conversion set explicitly does not. Substitutions require the intended function, measured suitability and actual fit.

fields.Declared contents: Broadback or another suitable host; Torque Bundle, Lowstep, Boxbrace and surface-appropriate feet.
fields.Why the combination works: Muscle supplies work, leverage delivers it and structure supports it. Protective carapace is an optional separate declared preparation.
fields.Breeding and commercial purpose: Cinderhouse suppliers can specialize in force, supporting material or repeatable kit dimensions. The whole set is not universally faster on a long smooth straight.
fields.Edition rule: A named set is a family of printed specifications, not ownership of particular source insects. A complete tin includes a host; a conversion set explicitly does not. Substitutions require the intended function, measured suitability and actual fit.

fields.Product purpose: Active aerial passing and recoverable landings.
fields.Declared contents: Complete Hoppers; suitable reserve; separately sourced Keel where included; required drive and contact declared either native or supplied.
fields.Why the combination works: Launch supply, release timing and landing recovery have different jobs. The original founder-style concept remains recognizable despite advanced preparations.
fields.Breeding and commercial purpose: Selected synchronized founders support premium development; useful intermediate Hoppers support ordinary tins. Third Friend is a complete-host edition, not a universal synonym for every Last Laugh conversion.
fields.Edition rule: A named set is a family of printed specifications, not ownership of particular source insects. A complete tin includes a host; a conversion set explicitly does not. Substitutions require the intended function, measured suitability and actual fit.

fields.Product purpose: Control the approach and reduce unnecessary rail loss.
fields.Declared contents: Moth-Felt Brake or declared Gripstrip alternative, plus supported Railshoes from a separate anatomical source.
fields.Why the combination works: The brake touches the approach; the guide touches the rail. Neither contributes its special effect when out of contact.
fields.Breeding and commercial purpose: Material specialists and fitters sell different value: friction and support come from stock, while engagement and exposure come from construction.
fields.Edition rule: A named set is a family of printed specifications, not ownership of particular source insects. A complete tin includes a host; a conversion set explicitly does not. Substitutions require the intended function, measured suitability and actual fit.

fields.Product purpose: Fast offensive racing with light protection.
fields.Declared contents: A light-carapace host, suitable drive and supply, working Catchclaws or Boiler, and actual support for each attack.
fields.Why the combination works: The racer still wins by completing the course. Attack timing and finite contents are part of the race, not a parallel elimination score.
fields.Breeding and commercial purpose: Arm breeders, valve specialists and high-delivery suppliers serve a distinct division. The exact offensive minimum is a sporting standard, not a demand for the rarest weapon.
fields.Edition rule: A named set is a family of printed specifications, not ownership of particular source insects. A complete tin includes a host; a conversion set explicitly does not. Substitutions require the intended function, measured suitability and actual fit.

fields.Product purpose: A complete aerial racer, not raised ground artwork.
fields.Declared contents: Host; Quadwing with working roots; flight drive and linkage; adequate reserve; sensory control; declared launch and landing contact.
fields.Why the combination works: Each source function survives the new locomotion: work, delivery, structure, control and energy. Passive browfoils do not stand in for powered wings.
fields.Breeding and commercial purpose: Pond rearing, intact emergence, flight preparations and transport cases support a full supply specialty. The reference exists before a flight runtime is built.
fields.Edition rule: A named set is a family of printed specifications, not ownership of particular source insects. A complete tin includes a host; a conversion set explicitly does not. Substitutions require the intended function, measured suitability and actual fit.

entries.title: One catalogue, several kinds of desirability

fields.Pattern name: Identifies a preparation or coordinated construction. It should be recognizable in anatomy and action.
fields.Breeder line: Identifies selected ancestry and its recorded objectives. It is not automatically owned by every shop selling its offspring.
fields.Printed edition: Identifies the contents, appearance and promises offered by a particular producer at that time.
fields.Performance band: Summarizes a declared measurement profile. It is not a price, a legal class or a historical authenticity claim.
fields.Collector variant: May be desirable for natural markings, packaging, provenance, restoration or a famous builder’s finish. A limited tin can contain ordinary excellent components rather than inaccessible superior genes.
fields.Historic recreation: Names what is original, retained, replaced or reproduced. A descendant host, an original winning animal, a revived donor line and a modern kit copied from an old sheet are different collectibles.

sections.title: 9. The hobby’s institutions and material culture
sections.intro: Institutions exist because they perform useful work for people with different interests. Their roles do not become exclusive player classes or biological permissions. Existing place and organization identities are retained.

fields.Role: An accessible Wrangloid counter centered on whole living insects, with prepared anatomy and coordinated kits alongside them.
fields.Practices and knowledge: Tank stock cards distinguish source, stage, visible condition, intended uses and the evidence the shop actually holds. The counter can demonstrate a component without pretending to know every wild animal’s ancestry.
fields.Livelihood: Buys ordinary stock and selected output, keeps useful breeders, commissions preparations and sells complete projects. Care, space and specialist knowledge make its work worth paying for.
fields.Boundary: Not a loot dispenser, genetics oracle or mandatory licensing office. Anyone can catch, breed or prepare outside the shop.
fields.Characteristic objects: Live-stock tanks, an intake bench, separated preparation cradles, illustrated tins and a small demonstration run make its different activities physically legible.

fields.Role: A cooperative breeder and supplier whose repeatable output supports independent Wrangloids.
fields.Practices and knowledge: Maintains separate research and supply objectives: a premium force/support line, ordinary kit stock, retained replacements and known useful preparation windows.
fields.Livelihood: Earns through suitable cohorts, selected founders and dependable dimensions or material properties. Finished kits can combine its stock with another supplier’s rather than require brand purity.
fields.Boundary: Not the owner of every retailer carrying its stock and not a universal authority that decides which insects may reproduce.
fields.Characteristic objects: Cohort racks, retained founder cases, comparative sample sets and shipping supports distinguish a broodworks from a decorative pet shop.

fields.Role: A recurring venue for assembly, practice, racing, demonstrations and social comparison.
fields.Practices and knowledge: Provides different services: free social advice, supported bench use, booked testing, named events and display space. Not every conversation is a contract or quest.
fields.Livelihood: Hosting, fitting and facility services can support workers and organizers. New entrants can borrow access to knowledge or facilities without becoming breeders first.
fields.Boundary: Only a declared qualifying event advances a championship. A display award does not secretly alter racing stats.
fields.Characteristic objects: Section shelves, repairable benches, timing desk, racer cases, trophies and a display cabinet connect everyday practice to public competition.

fields.Role: A live-stock broker and display specialist with customers who value appearance, provenance and unusual construction.
fields.Practices and knowledge: Keeps an asking-price claim distinct from evidence. A striking specimen can be valuable to a collector despite ordinary racing material.
fields.Livelihood: Commissions targeted searches, arranges consignments and finds appropriate buyers. A market for beautiful or historic stock does not require a universal fixed rarity price.
fields.Boundary: Not every inhabitant is wealthy, every offering is rare, or every trade is a championship upgrade.
fields.Characteristic objects: Individual cases, readable provenance labels, shaded display surfaces and careful packing show why a collector might travel there.

fields.Role: Transport living stock, prepared kits, personal racing cases and modular course sections between hobby communities.
fields.Practices and knowledge: Match the carried object to the journey: whole breeders need life-stage care, wings need clearance, living roots need support, dry shell preparations have another preservation class.
fields.Livelihood: Earn through scheduled capacity, careful handling and reliable arrival. A desired part can cost more in a remote settlement because reaching it requires actual work.
fields.Boundary: A departure receipt is not arrival. Carriers do not freeze every larva at its most profitable stage or make all towns instantly share information.
fields.Characteristic objects: Divided cases, articulated supports, route tags, receiving benches and handbill bundles connect materials and news on the same practical network.

fields.Role: A regional hobby publication connecting results, build features, field knowledge, arrivals and corrections.
fields.Practices and knowledge: Separates editorial observations, breeder claims, paid advertisements and owner-permitted construction disclosures. A photograph of a winner is not a genetic certificate.
fields.Livelihood: Helps people discover products, venues and desirable projects. Attention can lead to inquiries, but payments require actual agreements and delivered work.
fields.Boundary: Not a world-wide omniscient feed. Distant people learn through publication and distribution, not because a player opened a results panel.
fields.Characteristic objects: Issue covers, illustrated exploded builds, corrected stock notes, course sheets and signed results form collectible records of the hobby.

fields.Role: A builder who makes useful anatomy work well on a particular host.
fields.Practices and knowledge: Explains the requested result, supports the load path, maintains exchange boundaries, arranges physical fit and distinguishes restoration from inherited improvement.
fields.Livelihood: Earns through preparation, adaptation, measured fitting and maintenance. An ordinary component fitted well can justify labor without a promise of winning every race.
fields.Boundary: Expertise is valuable, but no profession unlock is required to attempt the work yourself.
fields.Characteristic objects: Root gauges, support cradles, sample preparations and annotated work sheets express practiced craft rather than futuristic machinery pasted onto every shop.

fields.Role: A craftsperson whose primary product is a distinctive, coherent-looking racer or collection piece.
fields.Practices and knowledge: Works with natural markings, shell finish, race identifiers, visible graft junctions and the selected silhouette. Maintains working clearance and necessary exposed surfaces.
fields.Livelihood: Earns for visual composition, restoration and commissioned identity. This is a valid output even when lap time is unchanged.
fields.Boundary: Beauty is not reduced to rarity or disguised as a speed buff. Decoration must not obscure the components a racing build needs its owner to recognize.
fields.Characteristic objects: Finish samples, masks, restored tins, lineage marks and before/after sheets record work and ownership.

fields.Role: People who turn owned sections, a place and a programme into a usable race meeting.
fields.Practices and knowledge: Build connected routes, secure supports, publish the important conditions and provide fair equivalent access under the announced format.
fields.Livelihood: Sell or loan equipment, perform setup, design memorable layouts and operate events. A great host can be celebrated without breeding a champion.
fields.Boundary: Cosmetic spectacle cannot conceal an invalid route. A familiar family of pieces can produce different layouts without making every construction a secretly scripted equipment check.
fields.Characteristic objects: Connector diagrams, counted section cases, raised-course supports, clear course cards and a results desk make the work visible.

entries.title: The common bench language is a practice, not a monopoly

fields.Purpose: Hobbyists can compare preparations and reproduce useful kits because they share vocabulary for source anatomy, measured behavior, fitting and condition.
fields.What it standardizes: A published pattern tells the recipient what is included, which body region it uses, what must be supplied and which settings remain adjustable.
fields.What it does not control: It does not own the mutation, ban raw grafting or require every independent invention to become a branded product before entering Open.
fields.Local variation: Communities can use regional names and different construction traditions while recording enough common information for visitors to understand the actual object.
fields.Commercial value: Reliable descriptions reduce unsuitable purchases and let an exceptional independent breeder sell beyond their immediate acquaintances.

entries.title: The hobby has a cycle without becoming an appointment game

fields.Local continuity: Practice, informal rivalries, retail and breeding continue outside the headline championship. A world-popular hobby cannot consist only of the player’s finite event list.
fields.Public rhythm: Stock releases, new course plans, qualification periods, display meets, traveling visitors and retrospective issues give the community reasons to return.
fields.Biological timing: Different donors produce useful stages on their own life cycles. Sporting demand can make a stage timely without causing the genes or insects to appear out of nothing.
fields.Access: Later race qualification controls entry to that competition, not the right to catch a donor or the existence of a superior trait.
fields.Player time: The default offline pause remains a participation principle. Specific schedules should create planning choices within the world, not punish the player for leaving the application.

sections.title: 10. The sporting world and the course as an object
sections.intro: Courses, equipment policies, qualification and competitive prestige define different things. The compendium describes the sport that the world can support; the limitations of an earlier two-roach experimental solver are not a limit on what the sport is.

entries.title: An event is described on independent axes

fields.Locomotion: Ground racing and sustained-flight racing use suitable routes and different performance demands. A winged silhouette is not enough to classify a flyer; actual locomotion is what matters.
fields.Equipment: Open permits unrestricted competitive constructions within the advertised course and basic validity conditions. Speedsters excludes dedicated weapons. Fireworks requires meaningful functioning offense and light protection. Each equipment policy can be stated independently of competitive standing.
fields.Competition: Local, Regional, Factional and world-level participation concern qualification and representation. They do not determine whether an insect can exist, be captured or reproduce.
fields.Format: A time trial, a single race, heats and finals, or a multi-race championship need their own announced rules. The earlier mirrored-pair programme is one experimental format, not the only possible event in a world-popular hobby.
fields.Result: The race requires valid course completion. Finish order determines a race victory. A championship can combine the results of its declared races; it does not silently become a damage contest.

entries.title: Equipment freedom and useful sporting boundaries
